title: How many games are you developing at once? And how?
author: HereToLearn321
selftext: And what is your general workflow like and tools you use? Describe kinda how you are doing things like your day to day, moment to moment.  What do you do while "waiting" or how do you structure your work ? What have you tried, disliked, liked, etc? Tools, etc.

comments.author: YKLKTMA
comments.body: If you’re developing more than one game at a time, you’re making a huge mistake

replies.author: Strict-Broccoli-8877
replies.body: I you're developing more than one game at a time, you are developing zero games.

replies.author: No-Marionberry-772
replies.body:
i think it really depends on what you mean.

I have a maun game project. For it ive been developing an engine.  the main project is large in scope.

In order to make sure the engine is solid and well rounded, i make small scope gamed to push on various boundaries.  I dont phone these small games in, because i want to be sure they are valid tests of the engines capabilities.

it does mean my process is slower, but i consider it a worth while effort.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: I’d say that building game engines and making games are two completely different tasks. If you’re trying to do both at the same time, you’re setting yourself up for failure.

replies.author: No-Marionberry-772
replies.body: its how many game engines came into being.  I used to very much be on the "why would I ever make a game engine" wagon,  after a few decades though, i see things a bit differently.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
You can’t build a modern-level game engine by yourself, so there’s no point looking back at how things were done 30 years ago.

Building your own engine only makes sense in very rare cases. For example, if you’re a huge corporation that doesn’t want to pay royalties on billions in revenue.

replies.author: No-Marionberry-772
replies.body:
I don't see what people did 30 years ago has to do with anything. However, I don't know why you feel the need to try to drag others efforts down.

You do you, I'm building my game engine which has been going quite well, and has a lot of time and effort behind it.

I think you probably really over estimate what a focused game engine needs compared to something that a single person is going to use. You might also under estimate what can be accomplished with AI automation and strong workflows.

Either way, you're not going to convince me to abandon years of work and knowledge.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
I’m not trying to devalue it. That’s just the reality of it. It’s like going to the Moon: most people have never been there and never will. A solo hobbyist can’t build a genuinely high-quality modern game engine, even with AI.

That said, building one can still be extremely useful for learning technology, especially if you really dig into the details.

replies.author: Crawling_Hustler
replies.body: No man, theyre r developing games. The workflow is called Slop factory. Now i know how there r so many fully AI generated games . I thought i guy would make one slop but i was soo wrong

replies.author: Fantastic_Ad_7259
replies.body: What about updates to existing games?

replies.author: Strict-Broccoli-8877
replies.body: Sure, fix bugs and do patches. But if you try to actively create new content for a game while also actively developing a second one - I will not believe you that there is a first game at all. Far above 99% of "Indie Developer" failures are because they lack the focus to finish one thing before they start the next. You have either developed this skill or you haven't.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: It’s generally better to avoid that. Updates only make sense if there’s a clear financial reason to do them.

replies.author: Level_Complex_4847
replies.body: Why? The agent is just doing it's stuff. Why not do more while you wait?

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: Even when you’re working on just one game, your mind should constantly be occupied with questions of design, playtesting, collecting and analyzing feedback, deconstructing games, and studying the reference games you’re using as benchmarks.

replies.author: ArchivisX
replies.body:
Hey, I'm one of those people making multiple games at the same time. I am not trying to ship anything at the moment. I'm just trying to refine my knowledge and skills with AI and game development. It's easy to prototype ideas for learning. Different games let me learn different things.

I am soon at a point where I've figured out most of the issues that I can start working on a legitimate ship-worthy project, but I didn't want to be one of those one-shot slop artists. I would focus on that exclusively when I do.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: The most valuable thing you can learn in game development comes from actually shipping commercial games. If you’re just making a bunch of half-finished games in a rush, nobody plays them, and you get no real feedback, then you’re basically wasting your time.

replies.author: ArchivisX
replies.body:
You're right, but I had to develop some skills that had gaps and I wanted to do so in a smaller environment.  I have 27 years of IT experience (enterprise sysadmin tier), so there are some things I am familiar/comfortable with.  I am familiar with shipping applications, just not games.

I am also building something at the moment for friends only since it uses copyrighted work.  I created a 90's era arcade that loads about 250 roms.  Each arcade cabinet loads its own artwork.  I updated the networking stack for the emulators to allow a server to act as the emulator host and it streams the game to players.  There's a virtual network layer that allows each person to sit at a stick and it works seemlessly.  The point where a player could get off Stick #1 and move over to stick #2 and someone else can step in without any interruption.  I fixed Gameboy Advance virtual link cable issues to allow similar stuff to happen.  I put other non-ROMs in my arcade (skeeball, air hockey, coin pushers, etc.).  I'm continuing to expand it.

Am I going to make money off it? no.  Am I learning a lot? Yes.  Here's a screenshot:

https://preview.redd.it/8befr9ntfwsh1.png?width=1617&format=png&auto=webp&s=885568b53401d53444fb744d4c02553b1ee922e9

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: I think you’re focusing too much on the technical side and losing sight of the actual product - the gameplay. You’ll never feel ready to make games if you keep going down that path, because the technical rabbit hole is endless.

replies.author: ArchivisX
replies.body: But I solved the technical problems already in this 'game'.  I'm now going over the lesser technical problems that require some more polish.  I'm starting to think you're more interested in being right than you are in engaging.  You got your upvotes already.  You don't have to prove anything to anyone.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: I’m not farming upvotes. I was just trying to warn you. It’s a common trap, and even large studios sometimes fall into it by pouring huge amounts of resources into technology they don’t actually need.

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body: I think it’s not a bad idea for people learning to have a few practice projects going on. I have my main game which I spend 80% of the time on and then little minigames/experiments just to learn different genres.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: It’s not just unnecessary, it’s also inefficient. As I said above, if you want to learn how to make games, you need to take them all the way to a commercial release and get real feedback. By spreading yourself across several games at once, you’re only slowing down your release cycle, which means you’re also slowing down your learning.

comments.author: Binoui
comments.body:
I've been working on the same game for 5 months. If you want quality, you can't rush it. Low effort vibecoded games are low quality games that nobody actually plays imo.  
Especially when you're solo, there's so much stuff that aren't just coding. Game design, product framing, visual direction, marketing, ... AI helps me in literally all those fields but if you delegate everything without input you get a forgettable result

comments.author: Carter5on
comments.body:
After my day job (9–5), I get home in about 30-40 minutes, prepare some food, and then pull out game concepts from my old notes.

From around 6 p.m. to 2 a.m. (sometimes 4 a.m.), I work on them with ChatGPT and Claude. I mainly use them for programming my 2D games, while instructing them to use programmer art (simple shapes, basic sprites, or other placeholders) during development.

I usually focus on defining and testing the gameplay first. Once a mechanic works, I move on to the next one, gradually building the game into something playable. Once the game has been properly defined and is playable, I start replacing the placeholder assets with my own artwork: UI, character and enemy atlases, level backgrounds, effects, and so on.

I should point out that I’m a professional UI/UX designer and an all-around game artist with development experience, so planning the project as a whole -gameplay, visuals, systems, UI, scope, and production- is relatively easy for me.

That’s basically my workflow at the moment.

Two of my games are currently in active development, and one has reached the point where I play it every day simply because I find it too much fun (I will need to post its demo on Steam at some point).

P.S. I only started using AI to help program my solo games this year, after getting tired of the headaches that came with doing all of the coding myself. My strengths are art, design, creative direction, and problem-solving during development. Programming has always been my weak spot. However, I am able to break a mechanic or system down into logical steps and understand how those steps need to work together. What I struggle with is remembering syntax and translating that logic into code.

Before that, I programmed my first four solo games myself in Godot 3 using GDScript and published them last year.

comments.author: aelindraonline
comments.body:
I'm working on one game full time. I use a combination of local and cloud computing, it sends off complex conversations to cloud and uses local for heavy grunt work.

I built a dashboard to see all of my processes and cron jobs running, 60+ currently. I can toggle them off and on at will which is nice because it saves me having to ask for it and burn model compute. 

I built in a GPU guard so if I'm gaming it never uses my local model and defers it to the cloud. 

I built a looping system which monitors context use in a session, and when it gets around 3/4 of context maximum it creates a log of where it currently is, opens a new session, self prompts the new one with the log, and kills itself.

I built a kanban board that the models and I use for task management and planning. We spent a few weeks heavily planning out what to do and when and why to realize the overall game. When the loop is turned on by me before bed or being afk for awhile it just completes task by task in order and keeps the kanban board up to date. I can come back from overnight for example and see an overview of everything it's done while I was away.

Everything lives in a private git repo and the structure of names and commit messages detail in ways a human can read easily and then a way for a model to scout and comprehend the data more easily for itself.

I added the ability for it to build all of the assets like 3D models and images using stable diffusion and Blender locally, i.e. most is grunt work. 

I have it build dev logs when we achieve anything meaningful and it maintains a Discord where we are testing social updates and auto moderation.

Before getting heavily into the game itself we spent most days or weeks making everything server authoritative, burning names we don't want players making their characters, integrated anti cheat and chat moderation and full character creation and in game management like item equip, inventories, battle systems etc.

I try to have it make scripts where possible that can be run over and over instead of passing something back to a model for it to work on, example would be town generator, you can build that to run in a script rather than having your AI do it every time with whatever formula you developed.

Still working on my game, it's like 1/100 done but all of the hard and boring stuff is almost out of the way. I just stick with the vision we worked on and try not to let things I read online steer me in a different direction or put me down. Most of this is because we can and we enjoy doing it, even if our games fail we are still doing something we get a great deal of satisfaction from and that's all that matters; if any of us can use AI for things like this, we should consider ourselves privileged, we are so lucky.

Best of luck 🤞

comments.author: Grouchy-Ebb-4168
comments.body: I tried working on a second game while working on my main game and it’s a failure, in the sense that it pulls you away from putting your heart and all into the main game. I always get a urge or a want to do more but you should just stick to doing one at a time and just make it as perfect as possible I aim for perfection that’s why my game stays above 4.8 in app stores

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
I usually work on two gaming projects at a time: one longer term and one demo/prototype. 

AI works really fast so technically I can work on 3-4 demos at the same time (it is just pointless since the demos/protoypes usually dont lead to anything besides reddit upvotes and I am just wasting usage limit)

I also capped my gamedev time so I can have time for reddit and gaming etc. I can still comfortably complete game projects in weeks. 

if you want to copy someone's workflow, start by copying the one-prompters' setups. They usually provide the full details of their workflow

if you are a more dedicated ai gamedev, you should be able to do better than the one-prompters. so treat their workflow and their result as a baseline and try to beat that.
